cards.front: Why put a queue between producer and consumer?
cards.back: Decoupling, absorbing bursts, faster responses and retries. The cost is that work is done eventually, so the UI must show 'processing' and you must monitor queue depth and age.
A work queue deletes a message once one competing worker processes it. A log keeps messages for a retention period, and each consumer group reads everything at its own offset and can replay.
Messages with the same key go to the same partition and stay in order; partitions are processed in parallel. At most one consumer per partition in a group, so partition count caps parallelism.
A write is acknowledged only once two in-sync copies have it, so losing a single broker loses nothing.

cards.front: Commit offsets before or after processing?
cards.back: Commit after processing for at-least-once delivery; commit before processing for at-most-once.
A queue gives each message to one worker, for work done once. Pub/sub gives each message to every subscriber, so several systems can react to one event and new consumers can be added later.

cards.front: Large payloads in Kafka or SQS
cards.back: Kafka's default max message is about 1 MB and SQS caps at 256 KB. Put large payloads in object storage and send a pointer.

At most once can lose messages, at least once can deliver twice (the usual default), and exactly once only holds inside a system that supports it end to end. Across systems, build it from at-least-once plus idempotency.
Processing a message twice has the same effect as once. Give each message a unique ID and record processed IDs, or write 'set to X' rather than 'add X'.

Write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction as the data, and let a separate relay publish outbox rows. It fixes the bug where a process dies between writing the database and publishing the event.
After a few retries with exponential backoff, move the message to a DLQ so one poison pill does not block workers forever. Alert on DLQ size and allow inspect and replay.
In SQS-style queues a received message is hidden for a timeout and reappears if not deleted in time. Set it longer than the slowest normal processing time, or extend it while working.

quiz.q: A Kafka consumer group has 3 partitions and 4 consumers. What happens?
choices: Each consumer gets 0.75 of a partition
The fourth consumer reads all partitions as backup
quiz.why: Each partition goes to at most one consumer in a group.

quiz.q: A worker finishes the work, then crashes before acknowledging. Under at-least-once delivery, what follows?
choices: The message is redelivered, so the consumer must be idempotent
The broker rolls back the work
The message goes straight to the dead-letter queue
quiz.why: Duplicates are expected with at-least-once, which is why consumers are made idempotent.

quiz.q: Which signal is best for scaling consumers and spotting backpressure?
quiz.why: The count alone hides how long work has been waiting; age shows the delay users feel.

quiz.q: An order service writes to the database, then publishes an event, and sometimes events go missing. What fixes it?
quiz.why: Writing the event in the same transaction as the data means a crash cannot lose it.

quiz.q: Search, analytics and billing all need every 'order placed' event. Which pattern fits?
choices: Pub/sub or a log with a consumer group per system
One work queue shared by all three
Synchronous calls from the order API
quiz.why: A work queue gives each message to only one worker, but each system needs every event.

choices: Strict order within a partition, by message key
Global order across the whole topic
quiz.why: Messages with the same key share a partition and stay in order.

quiz.q: Why move a message to a dead-letter queue after about five failed attempts?
choices: So one poison pill does not block or burn workers forever
quiz.why: Retrying a bad message forever wastes workers; the DLQ isolates it for inspection.
